renewal.note: 12-episode TV anime concluded June 28, 2015, supplemented by 2 OAD episodes. The manga by Miki Yoshikawa ran 28 volumes (2012-2017). A live-action drama aired in 2013.

bollymeter.basis: The 12-episode TV run adapts only a portion of the 28-volume manga, leaving core storylines unresolved. Reviewers found the body-swap comedy entertaining but noted the compressed adaptation pace works against the source material's character development.

seasons.review_body: Liden Films produced this 12-episode adaptation of Miki Yoshikawa's Weekly Shonen Magazine series for the spring 2015 season, with Crunchyroll simulcasting globally. The body-swap premise generates reliable romantic comedy mechanics - Yamada Ryu's rough-edged personality finding unexpected empathy through inhabiting his classmates generates genuine warmth. The seven witches concept is inventive, giving each character a distinct supernatural quirk that drives episodic plots while building toward a larger school-council mystery. The central liability is compression: the manga spans 28 volumes and the TV anime covers its first major arc in 12 episodes, leaving significant character work truncated. Viewers unfamiliar with the source material reported the ending as abrupt. The manga sold over 3.85 million copies in Japan as of 2017, demonstrating a fanbase the anime only partially served. A worthwhile introduction to the premise, with the caveat that the full story lives in the source.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A nimble premiere that drops Yamada into the body-swap mechanic quickly and mines genuine comedy from his reaction to suddenly inhabiting his studious classmate.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The accidental first body-swap down a staircase - played for pure physical comedy - is the scene that defines the show's tonal register.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Yamada Kun And The Seven Witches S1E1: "Why Are We Kissing?" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

Yamada Ryu begins as a problem the school already knows how to file: late, absent, asleep. Then he wakes into a worse attendance issue. His body is gone, Shiraishi Urara’s life is suddenly his problem, and the episode moves fast. The premiere works because it treats its ridiculous hook like a practical emergency before it treats it as a supernatural mystery. The kiss is funny. The rule-making is what gives it bite.

## The Slacker Becomes the Experiment

**Yamada Ryu** is introduced through discipline before personality. He arrives late, leaves early, nods off, and gets called out. That opening matters because the body-switch chaos lands on a boy already framed as careless with his own life. The first switch becomes a clean joke: the guy who can barely manage his own school day now has to manage someone else’s body.

His panic is the right kind of broad. Yamada’s cry, “I’ve turned into her!”, does the pilot’s bluntest job without apology. The line is inelegant by design. The episode needs the audience inside the premise quickly, so the writing chooses speed over coyness. Within minutes, the situation is named as a body switch, and the hour refuses to waste time pretending the characters cannot grasp the obvious.

That bluntness gives the premiere its engine. Yamada wants normal restored fast. The supernatural event is treated as a mess on a school day, not a chosen-one prophecy. His first instinct is repair. That is the show’s strongest early choice: the comedy comes from procedure, from two teenagers reverse-engineering an impossible accident with the seriousness of students fixing a broken phone before anyone notices.

## Stairs, Kisses, and Terrible Science

The staircase theory is the first workable rule, and the episode squeezes clean farce from it. Yamada and Shiraishi identify the fall as the likely trigger, then try to repeat it. The logic is foolish, but it fits the characters. They do not know the system yet, so they recreate the crime scene. Fall together, switch back, walk away. Easy.

Except it is not easy, and the hour finds its rhythm in that failure. The repeated attempts turn the premise from a single joke into a test chamber. The dialogue pushes forward. The actions get more desperate. The thought process narrows until the characters arrive at the last possibility: when they fell down the stairs, they kissed.

That beat is the pilot’s central comic pivot. The show does not spring the kiss as random fan-service noise. It makes the kiss a hypothesis. That sounds minor, but it separates a cheap gag from a plot rule. The episode’s title asks why they are kissing, and the script answers with dry logic: because the stairs did not work, and the mouth-to-mouth accident is the remaining variable.

The weakness is visible here. The early stretch is so dialogue-dense that the premise feels solved at sprint speed. The reprimand, the switch, the acknowledgement, the staircase repeat, and the kiss theory arrive in a tight chain. That pace helps a pilot, but it leaves little room for the strangeness to breathe. The episode is funnier when the characters test the rule than when they explain it.

## Shiraishi Draws the Line

**Shiraishi Urara** gives the hour its needed brake. Without her resistance, the premise could become a simple button: kiss, switch, chaos, repeat. Instead, the episode builds a boundary into the mechanism. Shiraishi wants the situation secret and controlled. She resists the idea of Yamada kissing someone else, and that objection matters because the rule is starting to expand beyond the two people who triggered it.

Here the pilot finds its best tension. The body-switch power demands experimentation. Shiraishi demands limits. The story roots those pressures in action rather than speeches. Once the possibility appears that Yamada might switch bodies with anyone he kisses, the plot gains teeth. A supernatural ability that works only between two confused classmates is embarrassing. One that can involve other people becomes dangerous, socially and personally.

Shiraishi’s stance also keeps Yamada from owning the premise by force. He may be the louder engine, the one trying to get back to normal quickly, but she controls the moral temperature of the hour. Her refusal turns the kiss from a gag into a consent problem the story cannot casually step over. That is a smart pilot move. The show keeps the absurdity while making clear that the rules will carry personal cost.

Her later agreement to join the club is a controlled compromise. She does not want the chaos free in the hallway. She accepts a room, a structure, and a title. In a school comedy, bureaucracy becomes damage control. Nice.

## Miyamura Turns Chaos Into Infrastructure

**Miyamura-kun** enters as the plot’s organizer. His interest goes beyond curiosity. The dossier points to student council aims, and the episode uses that angle to shift the body-switch business from private panic into institutional comedy. He offers the room. He requests involvement. By the end, the Supernatural Studies Club restarts, with Shiraishi as president.

That final movement matters because the pilot needs somewhere to put its premise after the first discovery. A body switch can power one frantic half-hour. A club can power a season. The room gives the characters a repeatable base. The positions give the jokes a social shape. The student council connection plants questions about oversight, access, and motive without making the episode heavy.

The quieter closing helps after the frantic middle. Once the switching outcome is confirmed again, the hour has proved its concept. The final job is to formalize it. The club restart does that efficiently, though the transition is compressed. Miyamura’s offer arrives late enough that the institutional setup feels brisk, almost too convenient. The episode earns the move in function more than emotion. It needs the room, so it gets the room.

As pilot architecture, the design is hard to argue with. Start with a delinquent problem. Add Shiraishi. Discover the switch. Identify the kiss. Introduce limits. Create a club. The show walks from accident to format in one episode, and the steps are clean.

## The Joke Has Rules Now

The strongest thing about “Why Are We Kissing?” is its understanding that a supernatural comedy needs rules before mythology. The open loops are clear: can the switch work with anyone Yamada kisses, what governs the trigger, and how will Shiraishi handle student council involvement now that the club exists? Those questions are planted through behavior, not dumped as lore.

That is why the premiere’s craft holds even when the exposition runs hot. Yamada’s urgency, Shiraishi’s boundaries, and Miyamura’s opportunistic structure pull the same premise in different directions. The episode asks whether a kiss causes a switch, then quickly moves to better questions: who gets to test that rule, who gets protected from it, and who benefits when the chaos gets a clubroom.

BollyAI’s read: this is a sharp, efficient opening with one real flaw. It hurries through its early revelations so quickly that a few reactions feel processed instead of felt. The trade works. The hour chooses momentum, and momentum is the right currency for this premise.

## The Verdict

“Why Are We Kissing?” is a strong pilot because it turns a silly magical accident into a working system by the final scene. The body-switch hook lands, the kiss rule gives the comedy a specific shape, and Shiraishi’s refusal to let Yamada experiment freely gives the episode a necessary ethical lock. The club restart is slightly too neat, and the early dialogue sometimes races past the emotional awkwardness of the situation. Even so, the structure is sturdy: accident, test, boundary, institution. As a season opener, it plants enough rule questions to pull the next episode forward without pretending the premise is grander than it is. BollyAI’s score: 7.7.

verdict.one_liner: A brisk pilot turns body-switch chaos into rules, jokes, and a clubroom before the premise can run out of steam.
